screens.title: Read what goes wrong without the rule.

blocks.p: Aoife is one of the shop's mechanics. She can only work on one bike at a time. Pádraig, at the counter, books a customer's bike in with Aoife for a full service at ten o'clock. A full service takes two hours, so Aoife is busy until twelve.

Ten minutes later Siobhán, on the other computer at the counter, books a different customer in with Aoife at eleven o'clock. Siobhán's screen does not know about Pádraig's booking. Now Aoife has two bikes for the same hour, and one customer is going to be let down.

The booking form cannot stop this on its own. Each form only knows about the bookings it loaded when it opened. The database sees every booking from every computer in the shop. So the check belongs in the database, inside the stored procedure that saves a booking.

screens.title: Remember the rule.

blocks.p: Why ask two questions instead of one? Asking only whether the new start time falls inside the old booking is not enough. A booking from 09:30 to 10:30 starts outside the 10:00 booking, but it still overlaps it. The two questions together catch every case: the same start, overlapping the start, inside, overlapping the end, and a long booking that covers the old one whole.
Touching is allowed. A booking that ends at 12:00 and another that starts at 12:00 do not overlap, because 12:00 is not before 12:00.

rule.text: The database refuses a double booking. The check is in one stored procedure, so every form on every computer that uses the database gets the same answer. You will type the two questions four times in this chapter, so that you can write them for your own tables without looking.

code.title: usp_Appointment_Add: save a booking, or refuse it
parts: The name, and what goes in and out

CREATE OR ALTER makes the stored procedure, or replaces it if it is already there, so you can run your script again and again. Each line that starts with @ is a parameter: one piece of information the form sends in. The two marked OUTPUT travel the other way. The stored procedure fills them in and hands them back.

AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts. The first job is to make @Message empty. An empty message means it worked. Every refusal below puts a sentence into @Message instead, so the program always knows which it was.
Work out when the job ends
The form only sends the start time. The ServiceType table knows how many minutes each service takes. DATEADD adds that many minutes to the start time, and the answer is kept in @EndTime.
Refuse if no service was chosen

If no row matched the service number, @EndTime is still empty, which SQL calls NULL. The stored procedure puts a sentence into @Message, and RETURN stops it right there. Nothing after RETURN runs, so nothing is saved.
Refuse if that is not a working mechanic
NOT EXISTS asks: is there no row in the Staff table with this number who is a mechanic and still active? If there is none, refuse.
Refuse a time in the past
GETDATE() is the clock right now. A start time earlier than now is refused.
DATENAME(WEEKDAY, …) gives the name of the day, such as Sunday. The workshop is shut on Sundays, so a Sunday is refused.
Refuse a time outside opening hours
CAST(… AS TIME) keeps only the clock part of a date and time. A job that starts before 08:30, or ends after 17:30, is refused.

EXISTS asks: is there any booking in the table for this mechanic, not cancelled, whose time overlaps the new one? The two overlap lines are the two questions from stage 1. The new one starts before the old one ends, and the new one ends after the old one starts. If any such booking exists, refuse.
Only a booking that passed every check gets this far. INSERT adds one row to the Appointment table, with the values the form sent and the end time the stored procedure worked out.
SCOPE_IDENTITY() is the number SQL Server gave to the row it just added. It goes into the OUTPUT parameter, so the program knows which booking it made. END closes the stored procedure.

GO is not SQL. It is a word for SSMS: run everything above this line as one batch, then start fresh. A CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE must be the first thing in its batch, so every stored procedure ends with GO before the next one begins. Leave GO out and the next one you paste fails with: CREATE PROCEDURE must be the first statement.
code.why: This test is the only thing between your diary and a double booking. Type it, so that you can write it again on your own tables without looking.

box.title: Before you log off: save your database

blocks.p: Booking 15 is a row in your database, and the Programming Environment wipes the database when you log off. Stage 7 cancels that booking. Whenever you stop before the end of this chapter, save the whole database, rows and all, to a script before you log off, as you did in chapter 3, stage 7, which also shows how to read the file:
1. In Object Explorer, right-click BikeShop, point at Tasks and click Generate Scripts….
2. Click Next, then Next again. Leave Script entire database and all database objects chosen.
3. Click Advanced. Find Types of data to script at the bottom of the General list, change Schema only to Schema and data, and click OK.

4. Click Save as script file. Click the … button beside File name, open your OneDrive coursework folder, type BikeShop-saved.sql as the file name and click Save. If Windows asks whether to replace the file, click Yes.
5. Click Next, then Next again. When every line says Success, click Finish.

At the start of your next lesson, open BikeShop-saved.sql the way you open BikeShop.sql (File, Open, File…) and press F5 with nothing selected, instead of running BikeShop.sql. Your database comes back exactly as you left it, test rows and numbers included. Keep adding new work to BikeShop.sql: it is still the master copy. Never type in BikeShop-saved.sql.

If red lines say Database 'BikeShop' already exists, BikeShop.sql was run first this lesson. In Object Explorer, right-click BikeShop, click Delete, tick Close existing connections at the bottom and click OK. Then press F5 in BikeShop-saved.sql again.

stages.title: Your turn: the same rule for bike hires

screens.title: Read how a bike hire is like a booking.

blocks.p: The hire shop has the same problem, with dates instead of times. A hire has a StartDate and an EndDate, which are whole days. A bike that is already out cannot be hired to someone else for days that overlap.

A live hire has a Status of Booked or Out. A hire that is Returned or Cancelled does not block the bike. So the clash test for hires looks at the Hire table, for the same BikeID, with a status of Booked or Out, and asks the same two questions with the dates.
The next screen gives you the hire stored procedure, usp_Hire_Add, with one part missing. It already looks up the bike, works out the cost and checks the deposit. You write the clash test yourself.

code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Appointment_GetFreeMechanics
    @StartTime     DATETIME,
    @ServiceTypeID INT
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @EndTime DATETIME;
    SELECT @EndTime = DATEADD(MINUTE, DurationMinutes, @StartTime)
    FROM ServiceType
    WHERE ServiceTypeID = @ServiceTypeID;

    SELECT s.StaffID, s.FirstName + ' ' + s.LastName AS FullName
    FROM Staff s
    WHERE s.Role = 'Mechanic' AND s.IsActive = 1
      AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT *
                      FROM Appointment a
                      WHERE a.MechanicID = s.StaffID
                        AND a.Status <> 'Cancelled'
                        AND @StartTime < a.EndTime
                        AND @EndTime   > a.StartTime)
    ORDER BY s.FirstName, s.LastName;
END
GO

code.title: usp_Appointment_GetByDay: every booking on one day, with names
parts: The name and the one parameter
This one takes a date and gives back a list of rows.
AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts. No @Message: a list is never refused.

a, m, c and st are short names for the four tables, given in the FROM and JOIN lines below. Each + ' ' + joins a first name and a last name into one column, named with AS. The number columns come too, hidden later, so the program knows which row is which.
JOIN ServiceType st ON st.ServiceTypeID = a.ServiceTypeID

Each JOIN pairs a booking row with the matching row in another table: the mechanic's Staff row, the customer's row and the service's row. ON says which columns must match. Three JOINs turn three numbers into three names.
Only that day, in time order
CAST(… AS DATE) throws away the clock part, so every booking on that date is kept whatever its time. ORDER BY sorts the rows by start time. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.text:
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Appointment_GetByDay
    @Day DATE
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT a.AppointmentID,
           a.StartTime,
           a.EndTime,
           a.MechanicID,
           m.FirstName + ' ' + m.LastName AS Mechanic,
           c.FirstName + ' ' + c.LastName AS Customer,
           st.Name                        AS Service,
           a.BikeDescription,
           a.Status,
           a.Notes
    FROM Appointment a
    JOIN Staff       m  ON m.StaffID        = a.MechanicID
    JOIN Customer    c  ON c.CustomerID     = a.CustomerID
    JOIN ServiceType st ON st.ServiceTypeID = a.ServiceTypeID
    WHERE CAST(a.StartTime AS DATE) = @Day
    ORDER BY a.StartTime, m.FirstName;
END
GO

screens.title: Read why a cancelled booking is not deleted, and type the stored procedure that cancels one.

blocks.p: A cancelled booking is not deleted. The shop needs to know that it happened: who cancelled, how often, and which customers never turn up. So a cancel is a change of status. The clash test ignores cancelled rows, which frees the slot. This stored procedure is short enough to type whole.

code.title: usp_Appointment_Cancel: mark a booking Cancelled
parts: The name, and what goes in and out
Only the booking number goes in. @Message comes back out.

AS and BEGIN mark where the work starts. The first job is to make @Message empty. An empty message means it worked. Every refusal below puts a sentence into @Message instead, so the program always knows which it was.
Refuse unless there is an open booking with this number
If there is no row with this number whose status is Booked, the booking was already cancelled, already done, or never existed. Refuse with a sentence.
Change the status and keep the row
UPDATE changes the status to Cancelled. The row stays in the table. The shop keeps its history, and the clash test ignores the row from now on. GO ends the batch, ready for the next stored procedure.
code.why: Typed whole. The check and the UPDATE both say the same two things: the right booking, and only if it is still open.

blocks.p: Every row below is a test the examiner would run. The ones marked Must be refused are the important ones. If one of those gets through, the rule is broken, however nice the diary looks. Do each one in your program, and tick it when you have seen it happen.

check.what: A booking in a free slot
check.how: New booking, a free mechanic, a free time. It appears in the grid.

check.what: The same mechanic, the same start time
check.how: Book it again for the same mechanic. Message: That mechanic already has a booking in that time.

check.what: The same mechanic, starting inside the booking
check.how: Start 15 minutes after the first booking's start. Refused with the same message.

check.what: The same mechanic, overlapping the start
check.how: Start 30 minutes before the first booking, with a service long enough to run into it. Refused.

check.what: The same mechanic, overlapping the end
check.how: Start 15 minutes before the first booking ends. Refused.

check.what: A booking that starts exactly when another ends
check.how: Start at the first booking's end time. Allowed: touching is not overlapping.

check.what: Another mechanic at the same time
check.how: The same time, a different mechanic. Allowed.
Cancel a booking, then book the same mechanic at that time. Allowed.
Move, keep the same time, press Move. Allowed.

check.what: Move a booking onto another of the same mechanic
check.how: Move it to a time inside another of that mechanic's bookings. Refused.
Pick a Sunday. Message: The workshop is closed on Sundays.
